```{python}
#| label: setup

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio
from IPython.display import HTML, display

# Design tokens, taken verbatim from the live app's stylesheet so the deck
# and the product read as one system.
PAPER = "#0e1116"
INK   = "#f5f2ec"
SLATE = "#1a2028"
GAIN  = "#2f7d6e"
LOSS  = "#a8442f"
BRASS = "#c9a227"
MUTED = "#8b929c"
GRID  = "#232a33"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# EVIDENCE.  Every number below is measured from the Ticker repository or
# quoted from its own planning documents. Nothing here is invented.
#
#   git log            21 commits
#   plan.md   Sec.10   per-phase estimates, written before any code existed
#   prompts.md         "The plan is 8-12 days of work"
#   cloc-equivalent    line counts by extension, node_modules excluded
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

PY_LINES, TS_LINES = 7963, 3033
TOTAL_LINES = PY_LINES + TS_LINES          # 10,996 -> "about 11,000"
TESTS = 291

# plan.md Sec.10 build order: (phase, low, high) in developer-days.
# These feed the totals only; they are never shown. The slide-5 chart regroups
# the same estimate by discipline (see DISCIPLINES), which is what gets read
# aloud, because a mixed audience parses "Deployment" faster than "Phase 6".
PHASES = [
    ("Phase 0 · skeleton",        0.5, 0.5),
    ("Phase 1 · data in",         1.0, 1.0),
    ("Phase 2 · live prices",     1.0, 2.0),
    ("Phase 3 · portfolio",       2.0, 2.0),
    ("Phase 4 · charts",          1.0, 1.0),
    ("Phase 5 · chat",            2.0, 3.0),
    ("Phase 6 · polish & harden", 1.0, 2.0),
]
PLAN_LO  = sum(p[1] for p in PHASES)          # 8.5 days
PLAN_HI  = sum(p[2] for p in PHASES)          # 11.5 days
PLAN_MID = (PLAN_LO + PLAN_HI) / 2            # 10.0 days

# Hands-on time, reconstructed from commit timestamps: gaps longer than
# 45 minutes are treated as time away and excluded, plus 30 minutes of
# lead-in per session. That gave 9.2 h; rounded DOWN to 9 so the claim sits
# at the conservative end of the measurement.
ACTUAL_H = 9.0
HOURS_PER_DAY = 8.0                           # one developer-day
PLAN_LO_H, PLAN_HI_H = PLAN_LO * HOURS_PER_DAY, PLAN_HI * HOURS_PER_DAY
PLAN_MID_H = PLAN_MID * HOURS_PER_DAY

SPEEDUP_LO  = PLAN_LO_H / ACTUAL_H            # 7.6x
SPEEDUP_HI  = PLAN_HI_H / ACTUAL_H            # 10.2x
SPEEDUP_MID = PLAN_MID_H / ACTUAL_H           # 8.9x
REDUCTION   = 1 - ACTUAL_H / PLAN_MID_H

# Chart type is sized for a projector, not a laptop: base 20px, ticks 17px.
# Nothing on a chart is allowed to be smaller than the deck's caption text.
pio.templates["ticker"] = go.layout.Template(
    layout=dict(
        paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
        plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
        font=dict(family="Instrument Sans, ui-sans-serif, system-ui", color=INK, size=20),
        colorway=[BRASS, GAIN, LOSS, MUTED],
        xaxis=dict(gridcolor=GRID, zerolinecolor=GRID, linecolor=GRID,
                   tickfont=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace", size=17, color=MUTED)),
        yaxis=dict(gridcolor=GRID, zerolinecolor=GRID, linecolor=GRID,
                   tickfont=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace", size=17, color=MUTED)),
        showlegend=False,
        margin=dict(l=64, r=28, t=44, b=56),
        hoverlabel=dict(bgcolor=SLATE, bordercolor=BRASS,
                        font=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace", size=17, color=INK)),
    )
)
pio.templates.default = "ticker"
rng = np.random.default_rng(20260907)
CONFIG = {"displayModeBar": False, "responsive": True}

def show(fig):
    """Emit a chart as plain HTML; plotly.js is loaded once from <head>."""
    height = fig.layout.height or 500
    display(HTML(pio.to_html(
        fig, include_plotlyjs=False, full_html=False, config=CONFIG,
        default_width="100%", default_height=f"{height}px")))

def menu_style(**kw):
    """Chart buttons, sized to be clickable and legible from a lectern."""
    base = dict(
        type="buttons", direction="right",
        bgcolor=SLATE, bordercolor=GRID, borderwidth=1,
        font=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace", size=16, color=INK),
        pad=dict(r=10, t=10), showactive=False, active=0,
        x=0, xanchor="left", y=1.18, yanchor="top",
    )
    base.update(kw)
    return base
```

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TARGET TIME: 0:50 — TOTAL 0:50]</span>
Good morning.

Over the last few weeks I built a working application. It's called Ticker — a live stock dashboard.

It pulls share prices straight from the market as they change. You enter what you've bought and sold, and it works out what those holdings are worth now, and what they've made or lost. There's also an AI assistant built in that can answer questions about it.

One thing up front: the portfolio you'll see is made up. The prices are real and the maths is real — the holdings are a test set.

And it's running on the internet right now.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[PAUSE]</span>

But the app isn't really the point.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[SLOW DOWN — THIS IS THE SENTENCE THAT TELLS THEM WHAT THE TALK IS]</span>

The point is *how* it got built. I didn't write the code — an AI did. What I want to show you is what that changes about the work.
:::

## What I was trying to find out

[One experiment, one question]{.kicker}

::: {.pull style="margin-top:0.3em"}
What can one person actually build now, if an AI writes the code?
:::

::: {.takeaways style="margin-top:1.1em;max-width:36em"}
[I'm not a **developer**.]{.take}
[So I picked something **real** — not a tutorial project.]{.take}
[Evenings and weekends. The AI wrote the code; I decided **what it should be**.]{.take}
:::

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TARGET TIME: 0:45 — TOTAL 1:35]</span>
Before I show you any of it, here's what I was actually trying to find out.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO THE QUESTION — READ IT OUT]</span>

What can one person actually build now, if an AI is doing the coding?

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO THE THREE LINES]</span>

Three things worth knowing before we start.

I'm not a developer. And that's the point — it's the whole reason the question is worth asking.

I didn't want a tutorial project. I picked something real, with real complications, that I'd actually use.

And all of it happened in evenings and weekends. The AI wrote the code. I decided what it should be, and whether what came back was any good.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[PAUSE]</span>

So — let me show you what I decided to build.
:::

[One screen · three things]{.kicker}

:::

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TARGET TIME: 0:40 — TOTAL 2:15]</span>
The idea itself isn't exciting, and that's on purpose. One screen, three things.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO EACH CARD IN TURN — DON'T READ THEM OUT]</span>

Watch prices move as they happen. Know exactly what the holdings have made or lost — the real number, not a rough one. And be able to just ask it questions, in plain English.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[PAUSE]</span>

Anyone here could have asked for those three things.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[SLOW DOWN]</span>

But underneath, each one is a completely different problem. Live data is one kind of work. Financial accounting is another. A safe AI assistant is a third.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TRANSITION — ASK THIS AS A REAL QUESTION]</span>

So how much is really under those three sentences?
:::

## Eighteen skills, one small app

[What a project like this normally needs]{.kicker}

::: {.chipgrid}
[Backend APIs]{.chip}[Real-time connections]{.chip}[Live event streams]{.chip}[React interfaces]{.chip}[Client state]{.chip}[TypeScript]{.chip}
[Database design]{.chip}[Schema migrations]{.chip}[FIFO lot accounting]{.chip}[Caching]{.chip}[Rate limiting]{.chip}[Containers]{.chip}
[Automated deployment]{.chip}[Cloud hosting]{.chip}[Login & sessions]{.chip}[Secrets handling]{.chip}[Design systems]{.chip}[Test engineering]{.chip}
:::

::: {style="margin-top:1.1em"}
::: {.pull}
In most organisations, that list isn't one person. It's a team.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TARGET TIME: 0:40 — TOTAL 2:55]</span>
Here's how much.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[GESTURE ACROSS THE WHOLE GRID — DO NOT READ THE ITEMS OUT]</span>

Eighteen separate skills go into that one screen.

I won't read them out — but look at the range. Keeping a live connection open to the stock market. Designing a database. The accounting method for working out gains. Logins, so that not just anyone can open it. Renting a server, getting the app onto it, keeping it running. Visual design. Testing.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[PAUSE, THEN SLOW DOWN]</span>

And those aren't variations on one skill. They're separate kinds of work — back-end, front-end, data, the AI, design, deployment, testing.

Plenty of people cover several. Very few cover all of them well.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TRANSITION]</span>

So if you gave this to a team, how long would they say it takes?

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[IF ASKED WHAT A CHIP MEANS — DO NOT READ ALOUD:]</span>

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[SECRETS HANDLING = THE PASSWORDS THE APP USES TO TALK TO THE PRICE PROVIDERS AND THE AI. THEY CANNOT SIT IN THE CODE, OR ANYONE WHO READS IT COULD RUN UP BILLS ON MY ACCOUNT. THEY LIVE ON THE SERVER SEPARATELY, AND I SET THEM BY HAND.]</span>

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[CONTAINERS = THE APP PACKED UP WITH EVERYTHING IT NEEDS TO RUN — THE RIGHT VERSIONS OF EVERYTHING — SO IT BEHAVES IDENTICALLY ON MY LAPTOP AND ON THE RENTED SERVER. IT IS WHAT STOPS "IT WORKED ON MY MACHINE".]</span>

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[FIFO LOT ACCOUNTING = IF YOU BOUGHT THE SAME SHARE THREE TIMES AND SELL SOME, WHICH ONES COUNT AS SOLD? OLDEST FIRST. IT CHANGES THE PROFIT FIGURE, AND IT IS HOW TAX REPORTING WORKS.]</span>

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[CLIENT STATE = REMEMBERING WHAT THE PAGE IS SHOWING YOU WITHOUT ASKING THE SERVER AGAIN EVERY TIME.]</span>
:::

## It started with a plan, not a prompt

[What got written before any code existed]{.kicker}

::: {.split}
::: {}
::: {style="padding-top:0.2em"}
[1,064]{.hero}

[**lines of plain English** — the architecture, how it should behave when things go wrong, and what "finished" meant. Drafted in a sitting, argued over, then treated as fixed.]{.hero-note}

[prompts.md]{.tag}[The rule that mattered]{.h4}

["Do not paste one giant 'build the whole thing' prompt. The plan is 8–12 days of work; a single request produces a large volume of untested code that all fails together, and you lose the ability to tell which part is wrong. Run one phase per session instead."]{.quote}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TARGET TIME: 1:00 — TOTAL 4:45]</span>
Nobody opened a chat window and asked for a stock dashboard. The first thing made wasn't code — it was a plan. A thousand lines of plain English: what it should do, how it should behave when things go wrong, and what "finished" meant.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[SLOW DOWN — BE STRAIGHT ABOUT THIS]</span>

And I'll be straight about how it got written. I didn't type all of it. I said what I wanted the product to be, and the plan came back drafted. My job was to read it, push back, and decide when it was settled.

Writing all that down is normally the slow, dreaded part — the thing that stops people ever starting. Here it was an afternoon.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO THE QUOTE — YOU CAN READ THIS ONE OUT]</span>

My favourite line in the project. Don't paste one giant "build the whole thing" prompt — you get a mountain of code that all fails at once, and can't tell which part is wrong.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TRANSITION]</span>

So instead of one big ask, I settled into a rhythm.
:::

## One phase at a time

[Seven phases · the same short loop each time]{.kicker}

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme':'base',
  'fontFamily':'Instrument Sans, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif',
  'flowchart':{'htmlLabels':true,'useMaxWidth':true,'curve':'basis','nodeSpacing':40,'rankSpacing':78},
  'themeVariables':{
  'background':'#0e1116','primaryColor':'#1a2028','primaryTextColor':'#f5f2ec',

flowchart LR
  BRIEF["<b>Describe<br/>one piece</b>"]
  BUILD["<b>AI builds it</b><br/>code + tests"]
  CHECK["<b>Automatic checks</b><br/>291 tests, every time"]
  READ["<b>I read it</b>"]
  SHIP["<b>Ship it</b><br/>live in minutes"]

  BRIEF --> BUILD --> CHECK --> READ --> SHIP
  SHIP -. "next piece" .-> BRIEF

  classDef human fill:#2a2415,stroke:#c9a227,stroke-width:3px,color:#f5f2ec
  classDef agent fill:#1a2028,stroke:#39424e,color:#f5f2ec
  class BRIEF,READ,SHIP human
  class BUILD,CHECK agent
```

::: {.pull style="margin-top:1.1em"}
Seven phases. Twenty-one trips round the loop.
:::

[Small pieces meant every mistake stayed small. And putting it live took minutes rather than weeks — so problems showed up while the work was still fresh.]{.caption}

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TARGET TIME: 0:55 — TOTAL 5:40]</span>
Five steps, and it really is this simple.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TRACE THE DIAGRAM LEFT TO RIGHT AS YOU TALK]</span>

I describe one piece — never the whole thing. The AI builds it and writes the tests at the same time. Then a set of automatic checks runs on its own — the tests, plus tools that read the code looking for mistakes. No person involved, and it's where the cheap errors get caught. Then I read it. Then it goes live.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO THE ARROW LOOPING BACK]</span>

And straight round again. Seven planned phases — and twenty-one trips round it in the end, because every fix went round too.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[SLOW DOWN — THIS IS THE VALUE POINT]</span>

What matters is the speed of that loop, not any single step. Small pieces mean every mistake stays small. And because putting it live takes minutes instead of weeks, you find out you were wrong while you still remember what you did.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TRANSITION]</span>

Now — one trip round that loop taught me something I was not expecting at all.
:::

## The problem I didn't know I had

[The decision that makes it feel live]{.kicker}

```{python}
#| label: rate-mismatch

DURATION, TRADES_SEC = 3.0, 300
N = int(DURATION * TRADES_SEC)
t = np.sort(rng.uniform(0, DURATION, N))
price = 187.40 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.006, N))

def coalesce(interval_ms):
    """The real rule: keep the latest price, send it at most once per window."""
    step = interval_ms / 1000.0
    xs, ys = [], []
    for e in np.arange(step, DURATION + step, step):
        taken = price[t <= e]
        if len(taken):
            xs.append(e); ys.append(taken[-1])
    return xs, ys

x250, y250 = coalesce(250)

def note(ms, n_out):
    """The chart's only annotation: headline, current setting, and the key."""
    return [dict(
        x=0.015, y=0.98, xref="paper", yref="paper",
        xanchor="left", yanchor="top", showarrow=False, align="left",
        font=dict(family="Bricolage Grotesque", size=30, color=INK),
        bgcolor="rgba(14,17,22,0.9)", bordercolor=BRASS, borderwidth=1, borderpad=14,
        text=(f"<b>{N} price updates in</b> &nbsp;→&nbsp; "
              f"<b style='color:{BRASS}'>{n_out} reach the screen</b>"
              f"<br><span style='font-size:20px;color:{MUTED}'>"
              f"sending at most once every {ms} ms &nbsp;·&nbsp; "
              f"<span style='color:{MUTED}'>grey = every trade</span>, "
              f"<span style='color:{BRASS}'>gold = your screen</span></span>"))]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=t, y=price, mode="markers",
    marker=dict(size=4.5, color=MUTED, opacity=0.45),
    hovertemplate="a trade<br>$%{y:.2f}<extra></extra>"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=x250, y=y250, mode="lines+markers",
    line=dict(color=BRASS, width=3.5, shape="hv"),
    marker=dict(size=12, color=BRASS, line=dict(color=PAPER, width=2)),
    hovertemplate="what the screen gets<br>$%{y:.2f}<extra></extra>"))

buttons = []
for ms in (100, 250, 1000):
    xs, ys = coalesce(ms)
    buttons.append(dict(label=f"  every {ms} ms  ", method="update",
        args=[{"x": [t, xs], "y": [price, ys]},
              {"annotations": note(ms, len(xs))}]))

fig.update_layout(
    height=530, autosize=True,
    annotations=note(250, len(x250)),
    xaxis=dict(title=dict(text="three seconds of one stock",
                          font=dict(size=19, color=MUTED)),
               range=[0, DURATION], showticklabels=False, showgrid=False),
    yaxis=dict(visible=False),
    updatemenus=[menu_style(buttons=buttons, active=1)],
    margin=dict(l=30, r=30, t=70, b=56),
    hovermode="closest")
show(fig)
```

[Illustrative of the ratio described in the project's guide, not a recording of real trades.]{.caption}

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TARGET TIME: 1:35 — TOTAL 7:15]</span>
This is the moment that surprised me most.

A popular stock like Apple has hundreds of trades every second.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO CHART — THE GREY CLOUD]</span>

That grey cloud is three seconds of it. Nine hundred price updates.

Now — your screen only actually redraws about sixty times a second. And every update makes the browser repaint the page, on the same thread that handles your clicks. Three hundred a second is way more than it can handle, so the work piles up and the tab stops responding.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[PAUSE — THEN SAY THIS PLAINLY, IT IS THE POINT OF THE SLIDE]</span>

I did not know that.

I asked for live prices. What came back was live prices *and* a fix for a problem I hadn't thought about.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO THE GOLD STAIRCASE]</span>

That's the gold line. Keep only the newest price, and send it four times a second. Nine hundred in, twelve out — and your eye can't tell the difference.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[CLICK "every 100 ms"]</span> Four times more often — and four times the load on every browser.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[CLICK "every 1000 ms"]</span> Once a second is cheap, but you can see it lagging.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[CLICK BACK TO "every 250 ms"]</span> A quarter of a second is what shipped.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[SLOW DOWN — THIS IS THE VALUE MESSAGE]</span>

On my own, I'd have wired the feed straight to the screen and watched it fall over on the first busy stock, with no idea why. Instead I got the version an experienced engineer would have built, first time.

It isn't just that it types faster than you. It brings knowledge you don't have.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TRANSITION]</span>

So — what did I actually end up with?
:::

## Four ways a bug turned up {visibility="hidden"}

[Because things still go wrong — the question is how fast you find out]{.kicker}

::: {.cols}
::: {.card}
[Automatically]{.tag}[The tests]{.h4}

291 of them, written alongside the code and run on every single change. Free, instant, and they never get bored.
:::
::: {.card}
[By reading]{.tag}[A leak every test missed]{.h4}

It kept every price it had ever seen and threw none away. All 291 tests passed — tests check that answers are right, not that memory behaves.
:::
:::

::: {.cols style="margin-top:0.7em"}
::: {.card}
[In production]{.tag}[A data plan that fell short]{.h4}

Only visible once real requests hit a real market. Fixed by adding a second supplier rather than paying to upgrade — **a one-file change**.
:::
::: {.card}
[By looking at it]{.tag}[A chart that died on screen]{.h4}

It asked for a colour by name, the name didn't exist, and it drew nothing. Every number was still correct. It took a screenshot to catch it.
:::
:::

::: {style="margin-top:1em;font-size:0.54em;line-height:1.5;color:#8b929c;max-width:40em"}
Three of the four only appear **after** it is live — which is exactly why shipping in minutes, not weeks, is worth so much.
:::

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[HIDDEN SLIDE — NOT IN THE RUNNING TIME. WAS 1:20. TO RESTORE: DROP visibility="hidden" FROM THE HEADING, PUT SLIDE 8'S TRANSITION BACK TO "BUT IT'S NOT MAGIC. PLENTY STILL WENT WRONG.", AND ADD 1:20 TO EVERY TOTAL FROM HERE ON.]</span>
I don't want to show you only the parts that went well. So — four real problems, and each one turned up a different way.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO TOP-LEFT]</span>

The first one, I never even saw. The tests caught it on their own, before it got anywhere near the live app. That's the best case — it costs nothing, and it happens while you're still sat there working.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO TOP-RIGHT]</span>

The second, nothing caught. I found it reading through the code. The app was hoarding every price it had ever been sent and never letting go of any of them — so left running long enough, it would fill the machine's memory and fall over. And every single test passed, because a test checks whether the answer is right. It has no opinion about whether the app is tidying up after itself. That one was only ever going to be found by a person reading.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO BOTTOM-LEFT]</span>

The third, I couldn't have found at my desk at all. The free price feed gives you today's prices, but not last month's — so the moment anyone asked for a chart going back, there was nothing to draw it from. You only find that out against a real market, in real trading hours. The fix was a second supplier for the history rather than paying to upgrade — and that was a one-file change, because of a structural decision made days earlier.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO BOTTOM-RIGHT]</span>

And the fourth — nothing was broken. Not one number was wrong. A chart asked for a colour by a name that didn't exist, so it drew itself in nothing, on a dark background. The app was working perfectly, and you simply couldn't see it. No test catches that. It took somebody looking at a screenshot.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[PAUSE]</span>

Three of those four only turned up after it was live. Which is exactly why the speed of that loop matters.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TRANSITION]</span>

So — after all of that, what did I actually end up with?
:::

About eleven thousand lines of code. Two hundred and ninety-one automated tests — small programs that check the software still works every time anything changes. And it costs about three dollars a month to keep running.

Prices move live. The profit and loss is worked out the same way your broker does it for tax. And the analyst can read your holdings and put a change in front of you — but it can't make one itself. It has no way to. You press Confirm.

## It took nine hours

[Same scope · same specification · measured after the build]{.kicker}

::: {.split}
::: {}
```{python}
#| label: time-comparison

# Two bars, no axis, no legend, no gridlines. The comparison IS the chart;
# anything else on it is competing with the only thing that matters.
y = ["The plan", "What it took"]
v = [PLAN_MID_H, ACTUAL_H]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=[PLAN_MID_H], y=[y[0]], orientation="h",
    marker=dict(color=MUTED, line=dict(color=PAPER, width=1)),
    error_x=dict(type="data", symmetric=False,
                 array=[PLAN_HI_H - PLAN_MID_H],
                 arrayminus=[PLAN_MID_H - PLAN_LO_H],
                 color=INK, thickness=2, width=12),
    hovertemplate="%{y}<br>%{x:.0f} hours<extra></extra>"))
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=[ACTUAL_H], y=[y[1]], orientation="h",
    marker=dict(color=BRASS, line=dict(color=PAPER, width=1)),
    hovertemplate="%{y}<br>%{x:.0f} hours<extra></extra>"))

# Figures sit clear of the error bar rather than butting against it, which is
# what `textposition="outside"` would do.
for label, xpos, ypos, colour in (
        (f"{PLAN_LO_H:.0f}–{PLAN_HI_H:.0f} hours", PLAN_HI_H + 6, y[0], INK),
        (f"{ACTUAL_H:.0f} hours",                  ACTUAL_H + 6,  y[1], BRASS)):
    fig.add_annotation(x=xpos, y=ypos, text=f"<b>{label}</b>", showarrow=False,
                       xanchor="left", yanchor="middle",
                       font=dict(family="Bricolage Grotesque", size=38, color=colour))

fig.update_layout(
    height=500, autosize=True, bargap=0.55, barmode="overlay",
    xaxis=dict(visible=False, range=[0, 152]),
    yaxis=dict(categoryorder="array", categoryarray=y[::-1],
               showgrid=False, zeroline=False,
               ticklabelstandoff=16,
               tickfont=dict(family="Instrument Sans", size=26, color=INK)),
    margin=dict(l=290, r=40, t=40, b=20))
show(fig)
```

## What actually changed {.center}

::: {.pull}
The distance between having an idea and having a working thing just got dramatically shorter.
:::

::: {.takeaways style="margin-top:1.1em;max-width:38em"}
[A prototype now costs **hours**, not a release cycle.]{.take}
[You can build across skills you have **not** mastered.]{.take}
[Being wrong got **cheap** — so you can afford to try far more things.]{.take}
[The scarce skill moved from writing it to **knowing what to build**.]{.take}
:::

::: {.notes}
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[TARGET TIME: 0:45 — TOTAL 12:50]</span>
<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[SLOW DOWN. THIS IS THE CLOSE — LET EACH LINE BREATHE.]</span>

So — four things are different now.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[POINT TO EACH LINE AS YOU SAY IT]</span>

A prototype now costs hours rather than a release cycle. Which means "let's just try it" becomes a reasonable thing to say, instead of something we say and quietly never do.

You can build across skills you haven't mastered. You still need to know what good looks like — you just don't need years in each one first.

Being wrong got cheap. If an attempt costs an afternoon, you can afford for most of them to fail.

And the scarce skill moved. It used to be writing the thing. Now it's knowing what's worth building.

<span style="color:#c1121f;font-weight:700">[PAUSE. THEN READ THE LINE AT THE TOP, SLOWLY.]</span>
:::
